subject: whats the more reasonable way to estimate fscores?

messages.author: 71bfb5f1e96782a8
messages.subject: whats the more reasonable way to estimate fscores?
parts:
Hi Phil,

i want to fix an IRT-model to a representative sample and then estimate fscores for another sample. I see two approaches for that:

1. estimate the model, then passing the new data to fscores with the response-pattern option or

2. estimate the model, fix the item parameter, release the GROUP parameter, reestimate the model with both data sets combined.

However, both fscores correlate very high (.999), but at the lower end there is a considerable difference between both approaches (.15 on the theta scale). Why is there a difference, when the item parameter are the same? which approach is the better one?

Thanks a lot!

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: whats the more reasonable way to estimate fscores?
parts:
On Thu, Feb 13, 2014 at 10:47 AM, <bea...@gmx.de> wrote:
> Hi Phil,
>
> i want to fix an IRT-model to a representative sample and then estimate fscores for another sample. I see two approaches for that:
>
> 1. estimate the model, then passing the new data to fscores with the response-pattern option or

This assumes that the calibration and scoring samples are from the
same population, and therefore have the same 'group' level IRT
properties (same means, variances, and distributions).

>
> 2. estimate the model, fix the item parameter, release the GROUP parameter, reestimate the model with both data sets combined.

I'm not sure I understand this approach too well. A more effective way
to observe the problem would be to estimate the model with a multiple
group approach, and constrain the item parameters across groups so
that they are invariant (no DIF). Then you could freely estimate the
group level parameters in one group, which would be made in reference
to the N(0,1) group.

Combining the datasets into one, while ignoring group membership,
effectively makes the model into a weighted average between the two
groups.

>
> However, both fscores correlate very high (.999), but at the lower end there is a considerable difference between both approaches (.15 on the theta scale). Why is there a difference, when the item parameter are the same? which approach is the better one?

It's possible the latent mean/variance are different for the scored
group, which pulls the estimated latent mean/variance away from
N(0,1). I'm not surprised they correlate highly at all, but the mean
of the scores can be farther away from 0 since the prior used in
certain fscores() methods (like EAP and MAP) take the group level
information into account.

Again, a multiple group approach may be more consistent than 2), but
approach 1) is certainly viable if the samples are truly from the same
population. Cheers.

Phil
